Vignette: Maya, Age 35

Maya grew up in a small city in Ontario, the kind of place where everyone knew everyone, and she spent most of her childhood performing in community theatre, certain from the age of eight that she was meant to be on stage. By her late twenties she had carved out a modest but real career — regional theatre, a few television spots, the occasional commercial — and she had learned to live inside other people's stories with a particular kind of ease. That ease is mostly gone now.

Three years ago, Maya was walking home from a late rehearsal in Toronto when she witnessed a man strike a woman repeatedly in the entrance of an apartment building across the street. The attack was sudden and savage. Maya froze on the sidewalk, phone in her hand, watching something she could not make her mind accept as real. She called 911. She screamed at the man to stop. He did not stop for what felt like a very long time. The woman survived, but Maya stood there until the ambulance came, watching paramedics work on someone whose face she had never seen before and cannot stop seeing now.

In the weeks that followed, Maya told herself she was fine. She returned to rehearsals. She hit her marks, said her lines, and went home alone to an apartment that had started to feel like a place she was merely visiting. She began checking the locks two, three, four times before bed. She stopped walking home after dark, then stopped walking alone at all after a certain hour, reorganizing her entire life around a set of rules she never quite articulated but enforced with rigid precision.

Sleep became its own ordeal. She wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart already pounding before she is fully conscious, the images from that night assembling themselves without invitation. She has learned not to fight it, which mostly means lying still in the dark and waiting. She is exhausted in a way that rest does not touch.

The professional complications are harder to talk about. Acting requires a person to access emotion on demand, to be porous and present, to let things in. Maya finds herself increasingly unable to do that without paying a cost she cannot always afford. During a production last spring, she was cast in a scene involving staged domestic violence. She got through the first rehearsal by dissociating so completely that her scene partner asked afterward if she was all right. She said yes. She did not go back. She told her agent she had a scheduling conflict, and she has turned down two similar roles since then, quietly restructuring what she will and will not consider without telling anyone why.

She describes herself as someone who used to be good at people. She was social, curious, the kind of person who stayed late at cast parties and remembered everyone's birthdays. Now she finds crowded rooms exhausting in a way that feels almost physical, like being pressed on from all sides. She has a few close friends she sees occasionally, but she cancels more than she follows through, and she has stopped explaining herself when she does.

What troubles Maya most, when she allows herself to sit with it, is the guilt. She was not hurt. She was a bystander. She made the call, she stayed, she did what she was supposed to do — and yet she returns again and again to the moment she froze, measuring the seconds between seeing and acting, convinced that something in her failed. She knows, on some level, that this accounting is not fair. Knowing does not seem to help.

She is here now, sitting across from her therapist with her hands folded in her lap, because a friend finally said the word out loud — trauma — and something in Maya recognized it before she could argue back. She is not sure what she is hoping for. She says she just wants to feel like herself again, and then she looks out the window, because she is no longer entirely sure who that is.
